Newly hatched Yellow-crowned parakeet chicks emerge from eggs incubated at a focal temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], a regime that yields a relatively short incubation period; the age at hatching, based on comparative data from the closely related red-crowned parakeet (Cyanoramphus novaezelandiae), is approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days]. At the moment of hatching, these altricial nestlings weigh a mere 4.4 grams [Ww0 = 4.4 grams], a remarkably low initial mass that underscores their extreme dependence on parental provisioning during the early nestling phase. This tiny hatchling mass is consistent with the general pattern observed among small-bodied parrots, where neonates are born at a fraction of adult size and must accumulate substantial tissue over the subsequent weeks. The energetic cost of sustaining such rapid early growth is significant, and the nestlings rely entirely on the food delivered by both parents to fuel their development. Field observations indicate that the parents make frequent foraging trips to meet the high caloric demands of the brood, a strategy that is particularly critical during the first week post-hatching when the chicks are most vulnerable.

As the nestling period progresses, the developing chicks undergo a well-documented series of growth milestones under the prevailing thermal conditions of the nest, which typically approximate the species' active body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. At this temperature, the fledging event, defined as the age at which the young first achieve sustained flight and depart the nest cavity, occurs at 52.5 days after hatching [tx = 52.5 days after hatching], a figure again extrapolated from life-history data on the congeneric Cyanoramphus novaezelandiae at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This extended nestling period reflects the substantial investment required to develop the flight musculature and feathering necessary for independent locomotion. During this phase, the chicks transition from a downy covering to a full set of juvenile flight feathers, a process that demands considerable protein intake. The parents continue to deliver a diet composed predominantly of seeds, buds, and arthropods, gradually reducing their provisioning frequency as the fledglings approach independence. The timing of fledging is critical, as it must coincide with periods of high food abundance in the surrounding forest to maximize post-fledging survival rates.

Sexual maturation in the Yellow-crowned parakeet follows a defined schedule once individuals have completed their post-fledging development and are living under typical ambient thermal conditions near the species' core body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Under these circumstances, the onset of puberty is observed at 157 days after hatching [tp = 157 days after hatching], marking the initiation of gonadal development and the capacity to produce gametes at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This relatively rapid progression to sexual maturity is characteristic of many island-endemic parrots, which often face unpredictable resource environments and thus benefit from an accelerated life-history strategy. However, despite attaining physiological readiness for reproduction at this early age, individuals do not immediately engage in breeding activities; instead, a period of social maturation and territory establishment typically intervenes. The first successful breeding event, or the age at first brood, is deferred considerably, occurring at 584 days after hatching [tR = 584 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 41.3 °C at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This delay between puberty and first reproduction likely reflects the time required for young birds to secure a suitable nest cavity and form a stable pair bond.

Reproductive output in the Yellow-crowned parakeet is moderate compared to other small parrots. Females typically produce a single clutch of 5 to 9 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 5 to 9 eggs per nesting attempt], and they raise only one such clutch per year [F_R_i = one such clutch per year], resulting in an annual output of 5 to 9 eggs per year [Ri = 5 to 9 eggs per year]. This annual reproductive strategy constrains the species' overall fecundity, though it may be an adaptive response to the seasonal availability of preferred food resources in their native beech and podocarp forests. The adult body mass at which females achieve this reproductive potential is approximately 40.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 40.7 grams], representing a substantial increase from the initial hatchling mass. Males, by contrast, attain a larger ultimate body size, reaching an average adult wet weight of 51.2 grams [Wwi = 51.2 grams], a sexual size dimorphism that is common among psittacines and may be linked to competitive advantages during mate selection or territorial defense. This difference in adult mass between the sexes becomes apparent during the late juvenile stage as growth trajectories diverge.

The maximum documented lifespan for free-living Yellow-crowned parakeets, recorded during long-term banding studies conducted under the species' typical active metabolic conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], is approximately 12.5 years [am = approximately 12.5 years]. This longevity is noteworthy for a bird of this body size and likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates characteristic of predator-limited island environments. Comparative physiological measurements indicate that the basal metabolic rate of adults, measured under standard respirometry conditions at this same body temperature of 41.3 °C, reaches a peak of 88.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 88.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns with allometric predictions for psittacines of approximately 50 grams at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This metabolic rate supports the energetic demands of their active, arboreal foraging lifestyle. The combination of a relatively long life, modest annual reproductive output, and delayed first reproduction situates this species firmly within a slow-paced life-history strategy, which renders it particularly vulnerable to environmental perturbations such as habitat loss or introduced predators.
